ACCT 2010.name: Introduction to Financial Accounting
ACCT 2010.description: Provides knowledge of core business concepts in financial accounting following generally accepted accounting principles. Emphasis on understanding the primary objectives, principles, and users of financial accounting, analyzing basic business transactions and understanding their impact on financial statements, and defining and identifying the basic elements and content on each financial statement.
ACCT 2010.prereqs: MATH 1030 or MATH 1040 with a grade of “C” or higher, Business students only

ACCT 2020.name: Introduction to Managerial Accounting
ACCT 2020.description: Provides knowledge of core business concepts related to selected financial accounting topics and basic managerial accounting, including basic financial statement analysis, the analysis of product, service and period costs, and the role of accounting in the planning and control of business enterprises. Emphasis on problem-solving skills supported by appropriate analytical quantitative and qualitative techniques for tactical and operational decision making.

ACCT 3010.name: Intermediate Accounting I
ACCT 3010.description: A comprehensive analysis of the practice of financial accounting and reporting by public corporations to investors, creditors and other users. Includes analysis of standard setting, accounting theory and generally accepted accounting principles. Emphasis is on the purpose of financial statements with a focus on income determination and asset valuation. Includes the use of spreadsheets.
ACCT 3010.prereqs: ACCT 2010 and ACCT 2020 with a grade of “C” or higher; or ACCT 5500
ACCT 3010.coreqs: INFS 1100 and FNCE 3050 or Graduate standing

ACCT 3020.name: Intermediate Accounting II
ACCT 3020.description: A continuation of ACCT 3010 with focus on liabilities, equity, and special areas, including cash flow statements, leases, pensions, income taxes, and earnings per share. Includes the use of spreadsheets.
ACCT 3020.prereqs: ACCT 3010 with a grade of “C-” or higher

ACCT 3110.name: Cost Accounting
ACCT 3110.description: Cost analysis for purposes of control and decision making. Analysis of cost behavior, role of accounting in planning and control, and managerial uses of cost Accounting data. Includes use of spreadsheets. Topics of current interest will be discussed, including activity-based costing.
ACCT 3110.prereqs: ACCT 2020 with a “C” or higher;  or ACCT 5500

ACCT 4110.name: Advanced Managerial Accounting
ACCT 4110.description: Application of advanced managerial accounting information for planning, decision making and evaluation. Topics of current interest will be discussed and may include analysis of pricing, cost allocation, balanced scorecard and capital budgeting that relate to corporate decision making. This course includes learning through technical content, cases, creation and use of spreadsheets and current scholarly research articles in cost related topics.
ACCT 4110.prereqs: ACCT 3110 with a grade of “C-” or better

ACCT 4210.name: Individual Income Tax
ACCT 4210.description: Analysis of basic concepts of federal income taxes such as income, exclusions, deductions, and property transactions. Concepts will be applied to actual situations by the use of tax return assignments. Focus is on individual considerations and planning.
ACCT 4210.prereqs: ACCT 3010 and ACCT 3020 with a grade of “C-” or above

ACCT 4220.name: Corporate and Partnership Taxation
ACCT 4220.description: Primary emphasis is on C and S corporations and partnerships. Basic analysis of planning and compliance of most forms of corporate and partnership organization, operations, mergers and dissolutions. Business planning. Issues related to state and local taxation may also be covered.
ACCT 4220.prereqs: ACCT 4210 with a grade of “C-” or higher

ACCT 4310.name: Introduction to Accounting Systems
ACCT 4310.description: An introduction to the elements in an accounting information system, one of an organization’s central information systems. Explores the newest technology and the accountant’s/financial analyst’s role in designing systems. Includes “Hands-on” projects designed to expose the student to various software tools commonly used by accountants and financial analysts.
ACCT 4310.prereqs: ACCT 3010 with a grade of “C-” or above; Business Students Only

ACCT 4410.name: Accounting for Governments and Not-for-Profit Organizations
ACCT 4410.description: The course provides an introduction to financial reporting practices in governmental and not-for-profit organizations. Emphasis is placed on how financial reports created by governments and not-for-profit organizations are used by internal and external stakeholders. Accounting issues specific to governmental and not-for-profit organizations will also be covered in detail. Necessary for CPA exam preparation.
ACCT 4410.prereqs: ACCT 3010 and ACCT 3020 with a grade of “C-” or above

ACCT 4510.name: Accounting Ethics and Institutions
ACCT 4510.description: An in-depth study of the technical and behavioral ethical standards existing for professional accountants in all fields, and of the political and regulatory institutions that affect the practice of professional accounting including the SEC, IRS, FASB, AICPA and state authorities. Prepares students for dealing successfully with ethical issues throughout their careers.
ACCT 4510.prereqs: ACCT 4600 with a grade of “C-” or above; Junior or Senior standing or COB Undergraduate Director permission

ACCT 4600.name: Auditing
ACCT 4600.description: A study of generally accepted auditing standards. Specific focus is placed on concepts of the auditing function for financial audits, professional standards that guide audit performance, and processes and formal procedures used to plan, perform, and complete an audit.
ACCT 4600.prereqs: ACCT 3010 and ACCT 3020 with a grade of “C-” or above

ACCT 4620.name: Advanced Auditing
ACCT 4620.description: Study of advanced theoretical and practical issues in auditing. Specific focus is placed on the application of auditing resources commonly used in practice. The course emphasizes case analysis, research, individual and team presentations, and classroom discussion.
ACCT 4620.prereqs: ACCT 4600 with a grade of “C-” or above

ACCT 4950.name: Topics in Accounting
ACCT 4950.prereqs: Junior or senior standing or COB Undergraduate Director permission

ACCT 4960.name: Internship in Accounting
ACCT 4960.description: Undergraduate accounting internship for business students.

ASL 1010.name: American Sign Language I
ASL 1010.description: This is the first in a related series of courses that focus on the use and study of American Sign Language (ASL), the language that is widely used by Deaf Americans. This course includes basic ASL vocabulary, grammatical structures, and in-depth cultural awareness. Non-manual behavior, ASL structure, and fluency are included to challenge students’ ability to increase expressive and receptive skills in ASL. Students are introduced to the cultural values, beliefs, and behavioral norms shared by those within the Deaf community. Course typically offered: Fall, Spring

ASL 1020.name: American Sign Language II
ASL 1020.description: This is the second in a related series of courses that focus on the use and study of American Sign Language (ASL), the language that is widely used by Deaf Americans. This course includes intermediate ASL vocabulary, grammatical structures, conversational behaviors, and in-depth cultural awareness. Non-manual behavior, ASL structure, and fluency are included to challenge students’ ability to increase expressive and receptive skills in ASL. Students are introduced to the cultural values, beliefs, and behavioral norms shared by those within the Deaf community. This course is designed for students who have completed a minimum of ASL I.

ASL 2110.name: American Sign Language III
ASL 2110.description: The third in a related series of courses that focus on the use and study of American Sign Language (ASL), the language that is widely used by Deaf Americans. This course continues to increase ASL vocabulary, grammatical structures, and in-depth cultural awareness. Non-manual behavior, ASL structure, and fluency are included to challenge students’ ability to increase expressive and receptive skills in ASL. An intermediate course designed for students who have completed a minimum of ASL I and ASL II.

ASL 2120.name: American Sign Language IV
ASL 2120.description: The fourth in a related series of courses that focus on the use and study of American Sign Language (ASL), the language that is widely used by Deaf Americans. This course provides the opportunity to develop and use stories and language activities in both receptive and expressive modes. Non-manual behavior, ASL structure, and fluency are included to challenge students’ ability to increase expressive and receptive skills in ASL. Offers a more in-depth discussion of the principles of ASL. Presents further exposure to more sophisticated dialogue.

ASL 3040.name: American Sign Language Fingerspelling and Numbers
ASL 3040.description: This course will aid students in developing increased fluency in their expressive and receptive abilities at ASL fingerspelling, one of the most difficult ASL skills to master, and aid in navigating the complex rules of ASL numbering. The course focuses on specific skills that underlie the fingerspelled word recognition process, and provides practice in correctly recognizing fingerspelled words and numbers in context. In addition to receptive skill development, students will hone their articulation and production of fingerspelling  and numbering. Taught in ASL.

ASL 3110.name: American Sign Language V
ASL 3110.description: This is the fifth in a related series of courses that focus on the use and study of American Sign Language (ASL), the language that is widely used by Deaf Americans. This course provides the opportunity to develop and use stories and language activities in both receptive and expressive modes. Non-manual behavior, ASL structure, and fluency are included to challenge students’ ability to increase expressive and receptive skills in ASL at an advanced level. It offers a more in-depth discussion of the principles of ASL and comparison of communication methodologies. Presents further exposure to more sophisticated dialogue.

ASL 3190.name: Introduction to American Sign Language Literature
ASL 3190.description: Provides students with an opportunity to recognize the impact of Deaf Culture on emerging ASL literature. The course also covers non-fiction, poetry, and drama depicted in reading and videotapes related to everyday lives of deaf people. It develops insight and appreciation of deaf literature and its implications for deaf education. Original works will be studied, analyzed, and compared. An intermediate course for students who have completed a minimum of ASL I, II, and III.

ASL 3490.name: Internship in Applied American Sign Language
ASL 3490.description: The Department of Languages and Cultures will offer to advanced language students the opportunity for supervised application of their knowledge in settings such as schools, social support agencies, etc. May be repeated up to three times for credit.

ASL 3500.name: Special Topics in American Sign Language and Culture
ASL 3500.description: Varying topics of current importance in linguistic and socio-cultural study. May be repeated once for credit if the topic is different.

ASL 3590.name: Deaf Culture
ASL 3590.description: Examines the culture of deaf people. The course will explore the customs, values, norms and heritage of the deaf community in America.

ASL 4000.name: Contrastive Linguistic Analysis: ASL/English
ASL 4000.description: Introduction to basic similarities and differences in the linguistic structures and uses of American Sign Language (ASL) and English. Examining categories from a universal perspective, contrastive linguistic analysis is accomplished by focusing on: phonological and morphological processes, syntactic properties, discourse types, word classes, and linguistic variation in Deaf and non-deaf communities in the United States. The student will also analyze both ASL and English language samples. Approved for LAS Cultural Diversity Requirement.

ANTH 1020.name: Introduction to Archaeology
ANTH 1020.description: Covers the basic concepts and methodology of archaeology using archaeological case studies from around the world. Approved for LAS Social Science area requirement. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirements: Explore-Society, Health and Behavior; Inclusiveness (Global/Diversity); Sustainability. Course typically offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

ANTH 1030.name: Introduction to Biological Anthropology
ANTH 1030.description: Evolution of humanity and its cultures. Covers primatology, evolution, race, biology, and prehistory. Approved for LAS Natural Science area requirement. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirement: Explore-Physical and Natural World. GT-SS3. Course typically offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

ANTH 1040.name: Introduction to Cultural Anthropology
ANTH 1040.description: Introduction to the major aspects of culture, such as social organization, religion, economics, language, sustainability, diversity, and cultural change. Approved for LAS Social Science area and Global Awareness requirements. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirements: Inclusiveness (Global/Diversity); Explore-Society, Health and Behavior; Sustainability. GT-SS3. Course typically offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

ANTH 2220.name: Experimental Anthropology
ANTH 2220.description: Experimental anthropology features student-picked projects including, but not limited to: replication of lithic artifacts, processing of animal hides, ceramic reproductions, replications of indigenous foods, rock art reproductions, etc., using authentic methods. Requires weekend activities.

ANTH 2230.name: Extraordinary Archaeology
ANTH 2230.description: This course introduces students to science-based archaeology by focusing on four or five extraordinary sites that have significantly changed the understanding of the past, and which can provide students with a feel for the range and scope of archaeological inquiry.

ANTH 2250.name: Introduction to Cognitive Archaeology
ANTH 2250.description: Course introduces students to the evolution and prehistory of the human mind through archaeological investigations of tools, hunting camps, living sites, cave paintings, engraved objects, figurines, ritualized burials, and personal ornamentation. Meets with INDS 2250, PSY 2250.

ANTH 2800.name: The Nature of Language
ANTH 2800.description: Introduction to the anthropological study of language. Approved for LAS Social Science area requirement. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirement: Explore-Society, Health and Behavior. GT-SS3.

ANTH 3000.name: Quantitative Methods in Anthropology
ANTH 3000.description: A survey of quantitative methods emphasizing the nature of hypothesis testing. Attention is given to special problems of bioanthropological, archaeological, and ethnographic data. Satisfies the LAS and Compass Curriculum Quantitative and Qualitative Reasoning requirement as a statistics course when taken by a student who has either 1) successfully completed MATH 1040 (or a mathematics course that has college algebra as a prerequisite), OR 2) scored 87% or higher on the College Algebra placement test and scored 50% or higher on the Business Calculus placement test.
ANTH 3000.prereqs: 9 completed hours in anthropology or consent of instructor

ANTH 3030.name: Why Science Matters
ANTH 3030.description: Course discusses how science works and its role in the modern world. Each term the course will focus on three or four issues of importance (e.g., climate change, evolution, relativity, death) and examine how science enhances our ability to understand and engage these phenomena. Meets with PSY 3020.

ANTH 3100.name: Special Topics in Anthropology:
ANTH 3100.description: Examination of selected topics in anthropology in lecture or seminar format. Topics will change according to the interest of the instructor and students. Students may repeat the course for credit as long as the topic is different.

ANTH 3150.name: Anthropology of Art and Expressive Culture
ANTH 3150.description: This course introduces students to the anthropological study of art, aesthetics and expressive culture by considering several cross-cultural examples. Students will examine how aesthetics express and inform about the cultures in which they are found.

ANTH 3180.name: Archaeology in the Public: Heritage Law, Ethics, and Community Engagement
ANTH 3180.description: Explores the role of government and public opinion in cultural resource legislation and ethics. Students will gain hands-on exposure to documenting and evaluating resource significance and will explore ethical considerations, descendant community engagement, cultural patrimony, and tribal rights.

ANTH 3190.name: Field Practicum in Applied Archaeology
ANTH 3190.description: A practicum course wherein students will work as part of a professional archaeological project and gain practical experience in archaeological field methods such as mapping, excavating, recording, survey, records and archives, field lab management, professional networking, and public consultation.

ANTH 3200.name: Special Topics in Archaeology
ANTH 3200.description: Intensive study of selected topics in archaeology. In different years deals with different topic areas.

ANTH 3210.name: Lab Techniques in Archaeology
ANTH 3210.description: Provides hands-on experience cataloging and analyzing materials from archaeological sites. Topics will include analysis, computer applications, materials conservation, and artifact illustration, and also the methodological decision-making that affects how we describe, analyze, and interpret data.

ANTH 3215.name: Mapping Archaeology
ANTH 3215.description: We will use Geographic Information Systems (GIS) to produce maps of archaeological sites, view the archaeological record from new perspectives, reconstruct past landscapes, perform spatial analysis on artifacts, and ask spatial questions of past human behavior.

ANTH 3220.name: Archaeology of Native North America
ANTH 3220.description: The archaeology of North America, emphasizing the peopling of the Americas, indigenous histories, and colonization.

ANTH 3240.name: The Archaeology and Genetics of the Stone Age
ANTH 3240.description: The cultural evidence for human development from the earliest stone tool assemblages of the Plio-Pleistocene to the Mesolithic and Archaic cultures of the old and new worlds.

ANTH 3250.name: Native Peoples of the Southwest
ANTH 3250.description: Explore the archaeology, history, and culture of indigenous cultures of the U.S. Southwest including impacts of colonization, resistance, and resilience. Approved for LAS Cultural Diversity requirement.

ANTH 3260.name: Agricultural Origins and the Emergence of Urban Society
ANTH 3260.description: The evidence for the origins of agricultural economies and the emergence of complex social and political institutions in both the old and new worlds. Approved for LAS Social Science area requirement.

ANTH 3270.name: Archaeology of the Recent Past
ANTH 3270.description: History and practice of the sub-discipline of historical archaeology. Students will explore diverse perspectives in public archaeology, and critically examine individual case studies. Approved for LAS Social Science area requirement. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirement: Explore-Society, Health and Behavior.

ANTH 3280.name: Archaeological Approaches to Gender and Sexuality
ANTH 3280.description: Course covers archaeological approaches to diverse systems of gender and sexuality in past societies. Students will analyze various case studies, spanning periods from the Paleolithic to the recent past.

ANTH 3290.name: Archaeology of Colorado
ANTH 3290.description: The ecological and geographical diversity of the State of Colorado has made it a rich source of archaeological research on its human past. This course covers the ways that archaeologists use material culture and landscape to study diverse cultural histories in the Centennial State.

ANTH 3300.name: Special Topics in Biological Anthropology
ANTH 3300.description: Intensive study of selected topics in biological anthropology. In different years deals with different topic areas.

ANTH 3310.name: Human Reproduction: Dating, Mating, and Parenting
ANTH 3310.description: This course will examine various facets of human reproduction, including anatomy, neurology, hormones, biology, and parenting. The information in this course will be based on a cross-cultural, evolutionary understanding of human sexuality. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirements: Explore-Society, Health and Behavior; Writing Intensive.
ANTH 3310.prereqs: ANTH 1030 or sufficient coursework in biology or health sciences

ANTH 3320.name: Primatology
ANTH 3320.description: Behavior, ecology, and evolution of nonhuman primates. Emphasis on field studies, and on evolutionary explanations of social groups, mating systems, and behavior toward kin. Approved for LAS Natural Science area requirement. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirement: Explore-Physical and Natural World.

ANTH 3330.name: Hormones and Behavior
ANTH 3330.description: This course covers the topic of behavioral endocrinology. Students will learn about various hormones, the role of those hormones in humans, and to a lesser extent, non-human animals, and the role of hormones in the study of behavior.
ANTH 3330.prereqs: ANTH 1030 or sufficient coursework in Biology or Health Sciences

ANTH 3340.name: Human Evolution
ANTH 3340.description: A detailed examination of the fossil evidence for human evolution, emphasizing functional analysis of human structure and the process of natural selection. Approved for LAS Natural Science area requirement. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirements: Explore-Physical and Natural World.

ANTH 3350.name: Forensic Anthropology
ANTH 3350.description: Explores the role of forensic anthropologists in crime scene investigation and mass disaster recovery. Students will learn to analyze skeletal remains to determine time since death, evaluate trauma, and identify age, sex, and ancestry.

ANTH 3360.name: Methods in Biological Anthropology
ANTH 3360.description: This course focuses on methods commonly used in the field of biological anthropology, exploring what it means to be human from the perspectives of our evolutionary history and our individual life Histories.

ANTH 3370.name: Human Biology and Ecology
ANTH 3370.description: The study of variation and adaptations of human populations in an ecological framework. Includes interactions between cultural and biological factors in health and in reproduction, and anthropological aspects of demography. Approved for LAS Natural Science area requirement. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirement: Explore-Physical and Natural World.

ANTH 3375.name: Humans on the Edge
ANTH 3375.description: This course uses a biocultural approach to explore the resilience of the human species looking at the ways that humans adapt biologically, physiologically, behaviorally, and culturally to survive and thrive in extreme environments and situations where few other animals can.
ANTH 3375.prereqs: Sophomore standing or above or ANTH 1030 or instructor consent

ANTH 3380.name: Evolutionary Medicine and Health
ANTH 3380.description: This course provides an evolutionary lens on human health. We explore data from biology, osteology, primatology, and cross-cultural studies to gain a holistic understanding of modem medicine and health. Topics include reproduction, cancers, aging, nutrition and energetics, and adaptive immunity. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirements: Inclusiveness (Global/Diversity); Navigate. Course typically offered: Fall, Spring

ANTH 3390.name: Bioarchaeology
ANTH 3390.description: Bioarchaeology focuses on the study of human remains from archaeological sites, both ancient and historic. In this class, we will learn the bones of the human skeleton, look at how health and behavior can be interpreted from human skeletal remains and explore case studies from around the world.
ANTH 3390.prereqs: Sophomore standing or ANTH 1020 or ANTH 1030 or instructor consent

ANTH 3400.name: Cultural Diversity in the United States
ANTH 3400.description: Examines the construction of diversity and perceptions of difference in the United States from a variety of perspectives. Provides students an opportunity to create a public-facing local research project. Approved for LAS Cultural Diversity requirement. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirements: Inclusiveness.
ANTH 3400.prereqs: Second-year student status or above; ANTH 1040 or permission of instructor

ANTH 3430.name: Anthropological Approaches to Globalization
ANTH 3430.description: Through specific case studies, seminar analyzes how cultural identities and societal changes both respond to and shape global agendas. Addresses innovative anthropological and ethnographic approaches to globalization studies, and considers why they form a critical component of contemporary anthropological research. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirements: Explore-Society, Health and Behavior; Inclusiveness (Global/Diversity); Sustainability; Writing Intensive.
ANTH 3430.prereqs: Second-year student status; ANTH 1040 or permission of instructor

ANTH 3450.name: Anthropological Approaches to Race
ANTH 3450.description: How has anthropology engaged with, produced knowledge about, and understood social conceptions of race and racism? Taught across the four sub-fields of anthropology, this course emphasizes disciplinary methods to track current directions in the study of race and racism. Approved for LAS Social Science area and Global Awareness requirements. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirements: Navigate; Writing Intensive.
ANTH 3450.prereqs: Sophomore standing or consent of instructor

ANTH 3460.name: Christianity and Freedom
ANTH 3460.description: This course is an ethnographic approach to analyzing how Christianity shapes and is shaped by questions of freedom. Students will read, compare, and critique scholarly accounts of Christianity both in the US and abroad. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirement: Explore-Arts, Humanities, and Cultures.

ANTH 3470.name: Environmental Anthropology
ANTH 3470.description: This course serves as an overview of the subfield of environmental anthropology. It explores anthropological approaches to understanding the relationship between humans and the environment.

ANTH 3500.name: Ethnographic Methods and Theory
ANTH 3500.description: Theoretical, case-oriented introduction to ethnographic research. Practical training provided in basic ethnographic research and analytical methods. Designed to engage students in grounded ethnographic research in the local setting. Research students design, conduct, analyze, and present as members of a team.
ANTH 3500.prereqs: ANTH 1040 and either ANTH 2800 or other cultural anthropology course

ANTH 3600.name: History and Practice of Archaeology
ANTH 3600.description: This course only offered in spring. A seminar designed for students who already have some archaeology coursework and are interested in the history and development of the discipline as well as trowel’s edge methodologies and theoretical debates.

ANTH 3660.name: Applied Community Studies
ANTH 3660.description: A service-learning, community-based research course in which students, professors, and community members work together to reach community-identified goals. Working in teams, students will learn to apply anthropology and human geography research methods in developing effective community outreach programs.
ANTH 3660.prereqs: two courses in anthropology, sociology, geography, or education, or permission of instructor

ANTH 3700.name: Special Topics in Cultural Anthropology
ANTH 3700.description: Intensive study of selected topics in cultural anthropology. In different years deals with different topic areas.

ANTH 3800.name: Special Topics in Linguistic Anthropology
ANTH 3800.description: Intensive study of selected topics in linguistic anthropology. In different years deals with different topic areas.

ANTH 3810.name: Language, Culture, and Society
ANTH 3810.description: An examination of the social and cultural functions of language, emphasizing the use of linguistic and cultural methods and theories in anthropology. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirement: Writing Intensive.

ANTH 3820.name: Native American Languages and Cultures
ANTH 3820.description: Examines Native American languages focusing on their cultural value in traditional/historic and contemporary contexts. Students study comparative linguistic typology of Native American languages, endangerment and revitalization efforts, and explore relations among Native American languages, cultures, nations, and bilingual needs. Approved for LAS Cultural Diversity requirement. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirement: Inclusiveness (Global/Diversity).
ANTH 3820.prereqs: ANTH 2800 or ANTH 3420 or WEST 3420 or WEST 2010

ANTH 3830.name: Language and Discrimination
ANTH 3830.description: Language practices and ideologies continually (re)produce forms of social difference and inequality within and across communities of interaction. This course examines the ways the semiotic landscape is intrinsically linked with political and economic structures and processes that aid in the establishment and perpetuation of language commodification and social differences. Throughout the course we will identify how racial inequalities are continually perpetuated in language use and practices. We will also explore how language can aid in the dismantling of social injustices.

ANTH 3970.name: History and Theory of Anthropology
ANTH 3970.description: This course is only offered in fall. History of the growth of anthropology and the questions it asks from the mid-1800s to present day.

ANTH 4040.name: Hunter-Gatherer Societies: Past and Present
ANTH 4040.description: In this course, we investigate the nature of hunter-gatherer societies from the archaeological and ethnographic points of view. Hunting and gathering was the only way of life for most of our past and this profoundly shaped our biological and cultural development. Approved for LAS Global Awareness requirement. Course typically offered: Rarely Offered

ANTH 4200.name: Advanced Topics in Archaeology
ANTH 4200.description: Intensive study of selected topics in archaeology and prehistory.

ANTH 4205.name: Wild Cognition
ANTH 4205.description: After appropriate academic and skills training, qualified students will spend several days in the wilderness using prehistoric techniques of hunting and gathering. At the same time they will be engaged in testing specific hypotheses concerning the cognitive challenges involved in these activities.

ANTH 4210.name: Advanced Laboratory Techniques in Archaeology
ANTH 4210.description: In this laboratory practicum, students analyze and interpret archaeological data and materials from the field school. Students will engage in specialized analysis techniques, data management and interpretation, report writing, and curatorial activities related to archaeological materials.

ANTH 4270.name: Landscape Archaeology: Sustainability and Collapse
ANTH 4270.description: Explore human landscapes at scales of research beyond the “site.” Survey perspectives from historically capitalist and pre-capitalist perspectives. Sustainability is the thread that ties this course together. Archaeology at regional scales explores environmental justice, ecology, and heritage. Approved for LAS Global Awareness and Social Sciences requirements. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirements: Explore-Society, Health and Behavior; Sustainability.

ANTH 4300.name: Advanced Topics in Biological Anthropology
ANTH 4300.description: Intensive study of selected issues in human evolution, human biology, and primate behavior and ecology. Different years deal with different topic areas.

ANTH 4310.name: Cognitive Evolution
ANTH 4310.description: Examines the evolution of primate and hominid cognition. Content includes basic neuroanatomy, relevant evolutionary theory, and neuropsychology (brain damage patterns), but the emphasis will be placed on the primate comparative evidence, paleoneurology (fossil endocasts), and the archaeological record. Open to Juniors and Seniors only. Meets with ANTH 5310. Course typically offered: Rarely Offered

ANTH 4320.name: Field Methods in Biological Anthropology
ANTH 4320.description: The purpose of this field course is to gain hands-on experience of a biological anthropology project in an international setting. The field of anthropology  has aimed to study humans from a cross-cultural, holistic perspective. International field work provides students with a first-hand experience of anthropological field work.
ANTH 4320.prereqs: ANTH 1030 or sufficient coursework in anthropology

ANTH 4330.name: Parasites in Human Evolution
ANTH 4330.description: What do sexual reproduction, immunity, and disgust have in common? PARASITES. Evolutionarily, our species has been in contact with microscopic animals that use us for shelter and food. How did this relationship evolve? Can we truly be healthy without them?

ANTH 4340.name: Primate Behavior and Ecology Methods
ANTH 4340.description: The course is designed to give students a working knowledge of primate behavioral ecology in a zoological environment. The objective of the course is to give students experience in major methodological aspects of primate behavior, data collection, exploratory, and confirmatory data analyses. This course will include an introduction to relevant statistical techniques.

ANTH 4400.name: Advanced Topics in Cultural Anthropology
ANTH 4400.description: Intensive study of selected topics in cultural anthropology. In different years deals with different topic areas.

ANTH 4420.name: Museums and Meaning
ANTH 4420.description: Students will critically evaluate the ways in which anthropology museums make meaning through practice. We scrutinize how museums can (mis)represent culture. We will focus specifically on issues of voice, narrative building, representation, authority, decolonization, and sensitivity. Approved for LAS Cultural Diversity requirement. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirements: Inclusiveness (Global/Diversity); Writing Intensive.

ANTH 4430.name: Labor & Social Transformation
ANTH 4430.description: This course is an advanced exploration into the theoretical and ethical dimensions of labor. It compares and contrasts categories of “labor” in order to highlight both the history of what labor is and the future of what creative attention to labor might enable in political and social spheres. Approved for LAS Social Science area and Global Awareness requirements.

ANTH 4440.name: Food and Empire
ANTH 4440.description: This course considered the people, process, and relationships whereby food serves as a channel for the exertion of power-linking moments of war, colonialism, and imperialism to the development of the American industrial food system. Approved for LAS Cultural Diversity and LAS Social Science area requirements.  Approved for Compass Curriculum requirement: Inclusiveness.

ANTH 4450.name: Ethnography of Sport
ANTH 4450.description: The course is designed to enhance student understanding of sport from an ethnographic perspective. The course introduces socio-cultural anthropological field methods including participant observation, interviewing, and narrative techniques and analysis of qualitative data.

ANTH 4515.name: The Archaeology of Numbers
ANTH 4515.description: This course examines numbers as systems comprised of interacting psychological, behavioral, and material domains, using concepts and evidence from psychology and ethnography to interpret the archaeological record. Course content includes the neuropsychology of numeracy, ethnographic behaviors with numbers, and ancient and modern numbers and counting devices. Meets with ANTH 5515.

ANTH 4650.name: Evolutionary Neuropsychology
ANTH 4650.description: This course serves as an introduction to the evolution of the structures and the functions of the human brain.

ANTH 4710.name: Internship in Anthropology
ANTH 4710.description: A program of study and learning outside the classroom. Practical exposure to field of interest is intended to provide appropriate experience related to a student’s career orientation. Students must have departmental permission. Anthropology majors only. Prerequisites vary depending on area of specialization.

ANTH 4800.name: Advanced Topics in Linguistic Anthropology
ANTH 4800.description: Intensive study of selected topics in anthropological linguistics. In different years deals with different topic areas.

ANTH 4980.name: Senior Seminar in Anthropology
ANTH 4980.description: This course offered only in spring.  A one semester special topics course designed to provide a synthesizing cap to the student’s undergraduate program in anthropology. Topics vary by semester. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirement: Summit.

ANTH 4990.name: Honors Thesis
ANTH 4990.description: For honors in Anthropology. a one semester research project. The student will write a formal research paper drawing on primary sources and pertinent secondary material. The student will work under the direction of a full time member of the department and will have a second member as an additional reader. The student will prepare an oral presentation to the faculty to include a thesis defense and responses to general questions in the four sub-fields. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirement: Summit.
ANTH 4990.prereqs: Senior status and consent of department chair

ARBC 1010.name: Beginning Arabic I
ARBC 1010.description: This course begins a sequence dealing with the development of functional proficiency in listening, speaking, reading, and writing the Arabic language. The course is conducted in Arabic. Emphasis is on communication in the language. Course typically offered: Rarely Offered

ARBC 1020.name: Beginning Arabic II
ARBC 1020.description: The second course begins a sequence dealing with the development of functional proficiency in listening, speaking, reading, and writing the Arabic language. The course is conducted in Arabic. Emphasis is on communication in the language.

ARBC 2110.name: Intermediate Arabic I
ARBC 2110.description: This course begins an intermediate level sequence dealing with the development of functional proficiency in listening, speaking, reading and writing the Arabic language. Conducted in Arabic with emphasis on communication.

AH 1000.name: Art Through the Ages
AH 1000.description: An introduction to the history of art and visual culture from around the world from prehistory to c. 1400. Course reading, writing assignments, and field trips (for in-person classes) equip students with the tools they need to think critically, write effectively, and build confidence in discussing art and culture outside the classroom. Approved for LAS Humanities area requirement.  Approved for Compass Curriculum requirements: Inclusiveness; Explore - Arts, Humanities, and Cultures. GT-AH1.

AH 1001.name: Global Visual Culture: 1300 to the Present
AH 1001.description: An introduction to the history of art and visual culture from c. 1300 to the present. Course reading, writing assignments, and field trips (for in-person classes) equip students with the tools they need to think critically, write effectively, and build confidence in discussing art outside the classroom. Approved for LAS Humanities area requirement. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirements: Inclusiveness; Explore - Arts, Humanities, and Cultures.

AH 1500.name: Introduction to Visual Culture
AH 1500.description: An introduction to the key issues in visual cultural studies through a broad examination of historical shifts in art and popular culture across time periods and geographies. Through course readings, writing assignments, and field trips (for in-person classes) students learn to effectively apply visual analysis and media literacy skills to interpret diverse forms of cultural expression, building confidence in discussing the politics of visuality and forms of representation from the development of perspective in the Renaissance; to photography and film; to video games and virtual reality in the digital age. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirements: Explore-Arts, Humanities, and Cultures; Writing Intensive. GT-AH1.

AH 2000.name: Survey: Special Topics
AH 2000.description: Selected topics focused on various historic periods of art history from throughout the world’s cultures. May be repeated for credit if the topic is different.

AH 2800.name: Survey: Ancient Art
AH 2800.description: A survey of sculpture, painting, and architecture from the Paleolithic through the Roman periods. The arts of Mesopotamia, Egypt, Anatolia, Greece, and Rome will be given primary consideration. Approved for LAS Humanities area requirement. GT-AH1.

AH 2810.name: Survey: Medieval Art
AH 2810.description: A survey of the arts of early Christian, Byzantine, early Medieval, Romanesque, and Gothic periods. Approved for LAS Humanities area requirement. GT-AH1.

AH 2820.name: Survey: Renaissance
AH 2820.description: Survey of the arts of Europe, c. 1400-1600, covering the Early Renaissance through Mannerist stylistic periods. Students study artists such as Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, and Sofonisba Anguissola. This course will also look beyond the confines of Europe to consider global connections, appropriations, and artistic influence during the “age of exploration.” Approved for LAS Humanities area requirement. GT-AH1.
AH 2820.prereqs: One AH 1000 level course or instructor permission

AH 2850.name: Survey: Art of the Americas
AH 2850.description: This course covers diverse topics in arts of the Americas. Specific course topics will change, ranging in time from pre-colonial to contemporary art, or surveying of the arts of North America, Mesoamerica and/or South America.
AH 2850.prereqs: One AH 1000 level course or instructor permission

AH 2860.name: Survey: Modern Art
AH 2860.description: An introduction to major movements in art and architecture from the late 19th to the mid-20th century. Art from Europe and the United States will be given primary consideration, beginning with Post-Impressionism and ending with Abstract Expressionism. Approved for LAS Humanities area requirement. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirement: Explore-Arts, Humanities, and Cultures. GT-AH1.

AH 2870.name: Survey: Pop Art to the Present
AH 2870.description: An introduction to major movements in art and visual culture across the world from the mid-twentieth century to the present, beginning with Pop Art and ending with a survey of contemporary trends.
AH 2870.prereqs: One AH 1000 level course or instructor permission

AH 2890.name: Survey: Eighteenth-Century Art
AH 2890.description: Survey of eighteenth-century European painting, sculpture, and architecture. Students explore the careers of painters including Antoine Watteau, William Hogarth, and Elisabeth Louise Vigee Le Brun as well as topics including Rococo and Neoclassical aesthetics, the Enlightenment, the Grand Tour, race, gender, and the art of revolutions. Approved for LAS Humanities area requirement. GT-AH1.
AH 2890.prereqs: One AH 1000 level course or instructor permission

AH 3000.name: Topics in Art History
AH 3000.description: Emphasizes study of a more specific area than that covered in regular art history course offerings. For further information see individual course listing for each semester.

AH 3010.name: History of Photography
AH 3010.description: The history of photography from its infancy to the present. The development of the photograph as art will be traced from the early 19th-century pioneers through the contemporary masters.

AH 3210.name: The Life and Works of Yoko Ono
AH 3210.description: This course examines the life and works of artist Yoko Ono through social, political, and historical contexts to gain insight on her art and music. Her biography, art theory and criticism published about her works, as well as creative and collaborative assignments will be explored. Approved for LAS Cultural Diversity requirement. Meets with JPNS 3210.

AH 3240.name: The Art of Greece and Rome
AH 3240.description: A consideration of the culture of ancient Greece and Rome as expressed by architecture, painting, and sculpture from around 800 B.C. to 400 A.D. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirement: Writing Intensive.

AH 3250.name: Women, Visual Arts, and Culture I
AH 3250.description: A survey of the lives and contributions of women artists, from the Renaissance to c. 1900. The primary objectives are to introduce issues of gender in the production of visual culture and familiarize the student with the critical literature of art history.

AH 3260.name: Women, Visual Arts, and Culture II
AH 3260.description: Introduction to feminist theory and women’s artistic production from 1970 to the present. Focuses on how women’s art attempts to resist normative ideals of femininity, subvert aesthetic hierarchies, and illuminates the intersections of race, gender, and sexual orientation.

AH 3270.name: From Modern to Postmodern Art
AH 3270.description: This course will examine the rapid change that characterized the art of the 20th and 21st centuries. We will begin with the emergence of cubism, dadaism, and surrealism in Europe, then shifting to American innovations, from Abstract Expressionism to graffiti.

AH 3280.name: Introduction to Feminist Film, Video and Digital Media
AH 3280.description: A survey of major themes in feminist independent film, video and web-based projects produced since the mid-1970s. Meets with WEST 3180.

AH 3330.name: Film, Video and the Avant-Garde
AH 3330.description: An examination of the relationship between avant-garde film and video, and the history of modern and contemporary art. Meets with FILM 3330.

AH 3430.name: African American Art
AH 3430.description: Introduction to contemporary (1970-) African American art forms with inclusion of traditional African art’s influence on American Black culture. Approved for LAS Humanities area and Cultural Diversity requirements.

AH 3450.name: Art of Japan
AH 3450.description: Examines the depth of Japanese aesthetics through layers of art and experience. In addition to sculpture, painting and ceramics, class material encompasses the artistry of the Tea ceremony, theatre (e.g., Kabuki, No & Butoh), calligraphy and textiles. Approved for Global Awareness requirement.

AH 3460.name: Islamic Arts
AH 3460.description: Investigates the essence and diversity of Islamic culture through time and space as it is visually expressed in architecture and other arts. Approved for LAS Global Awareness requirement.
AH 3460.prereqs: ANTH 1500, a course in Medieval art, Medieval history or by permission of instructor

AH 3790.name: Romanesque and Gothic Art
AH 3790.description: A consideration of Romanesque and Gothic culture as manifest in the sculpture, painting, and architecture of Europe from around 1030-1350.

AH 3840.name: Baroque Art
AH 3840.description: The 17th century throughout Europe with primary attention to Caravaggio, Rubens, Bernini, Poussin, Velasquez, and Rembrandt.

AH 3850.name: Topics in American Art
AH 3850.description: Selected topics in the art of America from colonial period to the present, including folk art, craft, modern art, post-modern architecture, monuments, popular art and culture, etc.
AH 3850.prereqs: A H 1000 or A H 2000 level survey

AH 3860.name: Contemporary Art
AH 3860.description: An in-depth, thematic study of art of the 1990s to the present that emphasizes the analysis of the art of our time in relation to a variety of critical texts. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirement: Writing Intensive.

AH 3920.name: Folk Arts, Folk Expressions, and Folkscapes
AH 3920.description: This course investigates different cultural expressions from belief systems to folk performances, vernacular architecture, and yard art where ingenuity creates senses of place, action, and performance. Includes visits to collections and folk art sites plus folk craft workshops. Meets with VAPA 3920.

AH 3980.name: Art History: Theories and Methods
AH 3980.description: This course will explore the history of art history as a discipline through an overview of common theoretical perspectives, methodologies and problems. In it, students will become acquainted with the theoretical and critical issues that currently dominate art historical scholarship and better understand the stakes of this field of study today.

AH 4000.name: Seminar: The Practice of Art History
AH 4000.description: Seminar experience in art history methodology. Required of all graduating majors. Open to students with 15 hours of upper-division coursework in art history.

AH 4030.name: Internship in Art History
AH 4030.description: Supervised opportunities for advanced art history students to apply their knowledge and obtain experience in a variety of professional arenas.

AH 4450.name: Meso-American Art and Architecture: Sacred Time and Space
AH 4450.description: Examines art traditions, cultural practices and the ethno-aesthetics of the Meso-American societies, Olmec, Maya and Aztec, in light of their history and subsequent European colonization. Different art forms are studied to understand the interdependency of art, ceremony, religious and royal display, cultural continuities, tradition and change. Approved for LAS Global Awareness requirement.
AH 4450.prereqs: AH 1000, AH 1500, or consent of instructor

AH 4470.name: Art and Ritual of the South Pacific
AH 4470.description: Investigates myriad art traditions and cultural practices of Polynesia, Melanesia, and Micronesia. Students learn to critique and analyze dynamics of power, cultural continuities and change. Examines ways art acts as a vehicle or catalyst for socio-political concerns. Approved for Global Awareness requirement. Meets with VAPA 4470.

AH 4810.name: Art of the Italian Renaissance I
AH 4810.description: A study of major trends in the development of painting, sculpture, and architecture as they reflect the culture of Renaissance Italy from around 1300-1500.

AH 4820.name: Art of the Italian Renaissance II
AH 4820.description: The late Renaissance and mannerism. The art of 16th-century Italy; special emphasis upon Michelangelo, Titian and Venice, both Florentine and Roman Mannerists, with some attention to Caravaggio.

AH 4830.name: Northern Renaissance Art
AH 4830.description: History of painting in northern Europe from the late 14th through the 16th century with primary emphasis on the art of the Low Countries.

AH 4890.name: Nineteenth Century Art I
AH 4890.description: History of the neoclassic and Romantic movements in European art with special reference to the Painting of David, Goya, Ingres, Gericault, and Delacroix, as well as consideration of architecture and sculpture from 1780 to 1850.

AH 4900.name: Nineteenth Century Art II
AH 4900.description: A study of the developments of Realism, Impressionism, Post-Impressionism, and Symbolism in France and England from 1850 to 1905.

AH 4910.name: Modern Art: 1900-1945
AH 4910.description: An in-depth, thematic study of the history of the avant-garde between 1890 and 1945 that emphasizes thee analysis of art of this period in relation to a variety of critical texts.

AH 4920.name: Art since 1945
AH 4920.description: An in-depth, thematic study of Modernism and Post- Modernism in the visual arts that emphasizes the analysis of art and architecture of this period in relation to a variety of critical texts.

AH 4980.name: Senior Capstone in Art History
AH 4980.description: This Senior Seminar is a requirement for graduation in the Art History concentration of VAPA. It is only offered in the Spring Semester and it is open to seniors and juniors. The senior seminar, or capstone, is a rigorous and demanding research course devoted to the development of your senior thesis. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirements: Summit; Writing Intensive.
AH 4980.prereqs: AH 1500 and junior or senior standing

ASTR 1050.name: Astronomy of the Solar System
ASTR 1050.description: The methods and results of modern astronomy (solar systems and stars) at an elementary level. Approved for LAS Natural Science area requirement. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirement: Explore-Physical and Natural World. GT-SC2.

ASTR 1060.name: Astronomy of the Universe
ASTR 1060.description: The methods and results of modern astronomy (solar systems, stars, galaxies, black holes, quasars, cosmology) at an elementary level. Approved for LAS Natural Science area requirement. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirement: Explore-Physical and Natural World. GT-SC2.

ATRN 4000.name: Foundations of Athletic Training
ATRN 4000.description: For students pursuing athletic training as a career. Foundational concepts for athletic trainers in prevention, recognition, and management of sport-related injuries and conditions. Also includes introduction to risk management and legal issues.
ATRN 4000.prereqs: HPNU 3050, HPNU 3060 (formerly BIOL 3050/3060 or BIOL 4350 or BIOL 2010/2020)

BIBL 1010.name: Introduction to Library Research
BIBL 1010.description: Introduction to the use of library services and research materials. Emphasis on the individual research needs. Designed for the undergraduate student in any discipline.

BIOL 1000.name: Biology in the Modern World
BIOL 1000.description: Designed for the nonmajor. The introductory principles of biology stressing the relationships between man and the environment. Concepts include heredity, evolution, genetics, nutrition, physiology, and ecology. Satisfies the LAS natural science requirement. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirement: Explore-Physical and Natural World. GT-SC2. To be taken with BIOL 1060 to satisfy the LAS laboratory requirement. May not count as credit for the major. Fall, Spring. GT-SC2.

BIOL 1011.name: Project Lead The Way - Biomedical Sciences
BIOL 1011.description: Students explore concepts of biology and medicine to determine factors that led to the death of a fictional person. Students design their own experiments to solve problems of human physiology, biology, and medicine.

BIOL 1012.name: Project Lead The Way - Human Body Systems
BIOL 1012.description: Students examine interactions among human body systems that result in muscle movement, reflex, and voluntary action and respiration. Students build organs and tissues on a skeletal manikin.

BIOL 1013.name: Project Lead The Way - Medical Interventions
BIOL 1013.description: Students learn and explore methods that prevent, diagnose, and treat diseases, including those that detect and fight infections, evaluate DNA sequence data, and evaluate cancer treatment options.

BIOL 1060.name: Introductory Biology Laboratory
BIOL 1060.description: May be taken in conjunction with BIOL 1000 to satisfy the LAS science requirement and lab requirement. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirement: Explore-Physical and Natural World. GT-SC1.

BIOL 1300.name: General Biology: Organismic Biology
BIOL 1300.description: The lecture component of an integrated lecture-laboratory course that presents the diversity of prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms emphasizing structure, function, ecology, and evolution. Students must also register for the laboratory, BIOL 1310.
BIOL 1300.prereqs: High school biology and chemistry, or consent of instructor

BIOL 1310.name: General Biology: Organismic Biology Laboratory
BIOL 1310.description: The laboratory component of an integrated lecture-laboratory course that presents the diversity of prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms emphasizing structure, function, ecology, and evolution. Students must also register for the lecture, BIOL 1300.
BIOL 1310.prereqs: High school biology and chemistry, or consent of instructor

BIOL 1350.name: General Biology: Introduction to the Cell
BIOL 1350.description: The lecture component of an integrated lecture-laboratory course that introduces concepts of the structure/function relationships among biological molecules, of cellular metabolism, and of genetics and molecular biology. Students must also register for the laboratory, BIOL 1360. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirement: Explore-Physical and Natural World. GT-SC2.
BIOL 1350.prereqs: CHEM 1401 or CHEM 1001 or CHEM 1201, and BIOL 1300/1310, or consent of instructor

BIOL 1360.name: General Biology: Introduction to the Cell Laboratory
BIOL 1360.description: The laboratory component of an integrated lecture-laboratory course that introduces concepts of the structure/function relationships among biological molecules, of cellular metabolism, and of genetics and molecular biology. Students must also register for the lecture, BIOL 1350. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirement: Explore-Physical and Natural World. GT-SC1.
BIOL 1360.prereqs: CHEM 1401 or CHEM 1001, and BIOL 1300/1310, or consent of instructor

BIOL 2030.name: Microbiology
BIOL 2030.description: Presentation of the basic aspects of microbiology within a broad biological perspective. Subject matter will include microbiological concepts and methodology; a survey of the distinguishing properties of microorganisms based on structural-functional relationships: introduction to growth, metabolism, genetics, and ecology. Fall. Spring. MUST ALSO REGISTER FOR BIOL 2130 – MICROBIOLOGY LAB.
BIOL 2030.prereqs: BIOL 1300/1310 and BIOL 1350/1360 or HPNU 2010 or HPNU 3050; CHEM 1201 or CHEM 1401/1402 or CHEM 1221

BIOL 2040.name: Project Lead The Way - Biomedical Innovation
BIOL 2040.description: Students build on the knowledge and skills gained from the three previous PLTW courses to design innovative solutions for pressing health challenges of the 21st century. Prer.; BIOL 1010, BIOL 1011, and BIOL 1013.

BIOL 2130.name: Microbiology Laboratory
BIOL 2130.description: MUST BE TAKEN IN CONJUNCTION WITH BIOL 2030. A series of laboratory experiments designed to illustrate the basic concepts of microbiology with hands-on experience. Fall, Spring.
BIOL 2130.prereqs: BIOL 1300/1310 and BIOL 1350/1360 or HPNU 2010 or HPNU 3050; CHEM 1201 or CHEM 1401/1402 or CHEM 1221

BIOL 3000.name: Biostatistics
BIOL 3000.description: An introduction to the principles, concepts, and processes involved in scientific research, with emphasis in biology. This includes study design, basic data analyses, data interpretation and evaluation of the scientific literature. Satisfies the LAS and Compass Curriculum Quantitative and Qualitative Reasoning requirement as a statistics course when taken by a student who has either 1) successfully completed MATH 1040 (or a mathematics course that has college algebra as a prerequisite), OR 2) scored 87% or higher on the College Algebra placement test and scored 50% or higher on the Business Calculus placement test.
BIOL 3000.prereqs: BIOL 3830 and MATH 1350 or consent of instructor

BIOL 3020.name: Cell Biology
BIOL 3020.description: Study of the structural and functional aspects of cellular life with emphasis on biological macromolecules, organelles, membranes, and cellular processes including respiration, photosynthesis, mitotic division and signal transduction.

BIOL 3100.name: Microbiology: Bacteriology/Mycology
BIOL 3100.description: Bacteriology/Mycology is an upper division, advanced study of the metabolism, physiology, and genetics of bacteria, yeast and fungus.

BIOL 3140.name: Microbiology: Virology
BIOL 3140.description: Virology is an upper division course covering the molecular genetics of viruses and their interactions with living organisms.

BIOL 3220.name: Animal Physiology
BIOL 3220.description: An examination of how invertebrates and vertebrates have met the problems of survival through physiological adaptations.
BIOL 3220.prereqs: BIOL 1300/1310 (formerly BIOL 1200), BIOL 1350/1360 (formerly BIOL 1210), and BIOL 3020

BIOL 3230.name: Plant Physiology
BIOL 3230.description: A comprehensive study of the physiology of photosynthetic organisms emphasizing molecular and cellular biology.
BIOL 3230.prereqs: BIOL 1200 or BIOL 1300/1310, BIOL 1210 or BIOL 1350/1360; prior or concurrent enrollment in CHEM 3101

BIOL 3300.name: Molecular Pathogenesis of Infectious Diseases
BIOL 3300.description: An examination of the molecular mechanisms utilized by medically significant eukaryotic microorganisms to cause disease. Emphasis will be placed on strategies for host invasion, immune evasion, and the molecular and immunological techniques used to explore these mechanisms.

BIOL 3610.name: Developmental Biology
BIOL 3610.description: Lecture. Examines cellular development with emphasis on vertebrate systems and experimental analysis.

BIOL 3700.name: General Ecology
BIOL 3700.description: A survey of environmental relationships of plants and animals. Topics include speciation, abiotic, and biotic limiting factors, population, community and ecosystem dynamics, and terrestrial and aquatic biomes. Spring (even years). Approved for Compass Curriculum requirement: Sustainability.

BIOL 3750.name: Conservation Biology
BIOL 3750.description: The major focus is the application of biological and ecological principles to preserve biodiversity. Ultimate sources and current worldwide losses of biological diversity are emphasized. Because conservation biology demands multidisciplinary approaches, historical, legal, economic, and ethical issues are also included. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirement: Summit.

BIOL 3830.name: Genetics
BIOL 3830.description: Molecular basis of heredity, gene expression and mutation with emphasis on meiosis and Mendel’s laws, linkage and recombination, chromosomal structure and aberrations, human genetics and quantitative approaches.
BIOL 3830.prereqs: BIOL 1300/1310 (formerly BIOL 1200), BIOL 1350/1360 (formerly BIOL 1210), CHEM 1401/1402 (formerly CHEM 1301 or CHEM 1030), CHEM 1411/1412 (formerly CHEM 1311 or CHEM 1060)

BIOL 3910.name: Immunology
BIOL 3910.description: A basic study of immunity which treats the biochemical, physiological, and genetic aspects of the immune response, particularly in humans.

BIOL 3930.name: Medical Ethnobotany
BIOL 3930.description: Introduction to the multidisciplinary study of medicinal plants. This course integrates concepts from ethnobotany, biochemistry, pharmacology, and conservation to explain the botanical and chemical basis of plant medicines, explore use of plant medicines by different peoples of the world, and define issues involved in contemporary adoptions of plant-based medicines.

BIOL 4000.name: Current Topics in Biology
BIOL 4000.description: Specialized topics and current issues are considered. Subject matter will change depending upon individual instructors. The topic in any given semester will be specified in the semester class schedule. May be repeated for credit more than one semester. Spring. Meets with BIOL 5000.

BIOL 4010.name: Seminar in Biology
BIOL 4010.description: This capstone course centers around the review and discussion of pertinent research subjects. Students will present seminars based on current research in the field. Fall. Spring. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirement: Summit.

BIOL 4170.name: Developmental Biology
BIOL 4170.description: An examination of invertebrate, vertebrate and plant development with attention to both classical and modern molecular genetic experimental techniques.

BIOL 4200.name: Developmental Neurobiology
BIOL 4200.description: Lecture. This course focuses on recent advances in understanding the molecular genetic and cellular mechanisms underlying nervous system development. This course introduces students to contemporary approaches for the study of neural development, emphasizing genetic and molecular techniques.

BIOL 4220.name: Epidemiology
BIOL 4220.description: An introduction to the basic principles and methods for studying human disease and improving public health.

BIOL 4250.name: Evolution
BIOL 4250.description: An introduction to evolutionary biology focusing on the principle of common descent and mechanisms responsible for generating the amazing diversity of life.

BIOL 4280.name: Mammalogy
BIOL 4280.description: Lecture, lab, and field studies. Origin, evolution and adaptation, geographic distribution, ecology, and taxonomy of mammals. Fall.

BIOL 4290.name: Plant Communities of Colorado
BIOL 4290.description: An examination of plant assemblages in Colorado. Major plant communities will be examined in the context of environmental factors such as climate and landforms. Required field trip.

BIOL 4420.name: Behavioral Ecology
BIOL 4420.description: The study of animal behavior from an evolutionary perspective. Examines the adaptive significance of behaviors involved in survival, foraging, habitat selection, reproduction, and social interactions in animals ranging from insects to humans.

BIOL 4460.name: Methods in Field Ecology
BIOL 4460.description: Introduction to biological research on the interactions among organisms and their environments. This course emphasizes field work in a variety of systems including soils, plants, insects, vertebrates, and aquatic biology.
BIOL 4460.prereqs: BIOL 1300, BIOL 1310, BIOL 1350, BIOL 1360, or by permission of the instructor

BIOL 4610.name: Methods in Evolutionary Genetics
BIOL 4610.description: This course is concerned with understanding evolutionary patterns and processes at the genetic level. Students learn principles behind methods used in the field and gain hands-on experience with techniques such as Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR), gene sequencing, gene expression analysis, and bioinformatics.

BIOL 4670.name: Applied Molecular Genetics
BIOL 4670.description: Learn how fundamental principles of chemistry and biology are applied to modern day biotechnologies. Examine the chemical and biological properties of nucleic acids, proteins and restriction enzymes and how they are used to clone genes, characterize proteins and discover drugs.
BIOL 4670.prereqs: BIOL 3830 and 3020, or by consent of instructor

BIOL 4710.name: Externship in Biology
BIOL 4710.description: A program of study and learning outside the classroom. Practical exposure to field of interest is intended to provide appropriate experience to a student’s career orientation. A variety of opportunities exists, and students may explore their own avenues as well. Some externships are in open competition. Students must have departmental permission and completed permission form to register. It is necessary for students interested in this program to plan their participation one semester before they plan to enroll. (Note: Externship is to be performed off campus at an institution performing biologically-oriented work, e.g., medical clinics and research laboratories.) Students must speak with faculty before registering for all externships. Fall, Spring. Course typically offered: Fall, Spring

BIOL 4830.name: Explorations in Genetics- Discussion and Lab
BIOL 4830.description: A lab and discussion exploring genetics topics and techniques. This class covers Mendelian and non-Mendelian inheritance, genetic engineering, model organisms, and applications of genetics. Includes experimental design and implementation, data acquisition, reading and analysis of primary literature. Students must take both discussion and lab sections concurrently.
BIOL 4830.coreqs: BIOL 3830 or BIOL 3020 with permission of instructor

BIOL 4840.name: Molecular Biology
BIOL 4840.description: Focuses on the biochemistry and techniques used to study prokaryotic and eukaryotic gene expression and regulation. Topics include transcription, translation, and transposition.

BUAD 1000.name: Introduction to Business
BUAD 1000.description: Familiarizes students with the structure, operations, management, and socioeconomic aspects of business and non business entities. Course builds on the college themes of entrepreneurship, technology, team building, and international competitiveness to establish a foundation for integrating information encountered in more advanced business courses. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirement: Explore-Society, Health and Behavior.

BUAD 1010.name: Building a Successful Future in Business
BUAD 1010.description: Learn the keys to success as a business student and in your future business career. Hear directly from employers, alumni, students, faculty, and advisors about potential careers, majors, and expectations on the job and in the classroom. Course will include presentations, discussions, exercises, and assignments designed to help you learn and practice skills that will set you on the path to success. This course is designed for new freshmen students.

BUAD 2950.name: Topics in Business
BUAD 2950.description: Experimental courses offered irregularly at the Sophomore level for the purpose of presenting new subject matter in a particular business field. Course prerequisites will vary depending upon topics covered.

BUAD 2960.name: Introductory Internship in Business
BUAD 2960.description: Undergraduate lower division internship for business students. Designed to encourage career exploration and development.
BUAD 2960.prereqs: INFS 1100, Business students only, Sophomore standing

BUAD 3010.name: Career Strengths: Assessment and Development
BUAD 3010.description: Gives students an in-depth understanding of their interests, skills, and values and how these match to particular jobs and professions. Through research and analysis the students will gain a clear, detailed picture of what they want to do and what they have to offer an employer. Satisfactory/Unsatisfactory only.

BUAD 3020.name: Career Skills: Resume Writing and Interviewing
BUAD 3020.description: Instructs and gives students hands-on experience on how to: (a) write cover letters and resumes, (b) practice effective interviewing techniques, and (c)develop effective job hunting skills. Satisfactory/Unsatisfactory only.

BUAD 3030.name: Career Success: Image and Impact
BUAD 3030.description: Helps students converse, interact, and dress in a professional manner for job interviews, telephone calls, written correspondence, and professional work settings. Course will cover working in a diverse, cross-cultural environment, making effective first impressions, and appropriately communicating in a variety of speaking and writing situations. Satisfactory/Unsatisfactory only.

BUAD 3100.name: ROAR Program I
BUAD 3100.description: Phase I of the ROAR Program - Find your ROAR. This course provides students with an understanding of their interests, skills, and values and helps them identify career pathways. Through research and self-assessment, students will learn about various career opportunities in business and develop a career plan.
BUAD 3100.prereqs: Score of 18+ on the English ACT; or score of 470+ on the Reading+Writing SAT; or ENGL 99; or ENGL 1305 or ENGL 1308 or ENGL 1310 or ENGL 1410

BUAD 3200.name: ROAR Program II
BUAD 3200.description: Phase II of the ROAR Program - Refine your ROAR. This course provides students with opportunities to confirm their desired career pathway. This includes industry panels, informational interviews, and industry tours. Students will also learn the basics of resume writing, interview preparation, and internship/job search to ensure they are ready for experiential learning opportunities.
BUAD 3200.prereqs: BUAD 3100; College of Business students only

BUAD 3300.name: ROAR Program III
BUAD 3300.description: Phase III of the ROAR Program - Ready to ROAR. This course aids in the transition from college to career. Students will engage in a variety of activities with industry experts to develop professionalism and networking skills.
BUAD 3300.prereqs: BUAD 3200; College of Business students only

BUAD 3600.name: The AI Advantage: Elevating Your Career Path
BUAD 3600.description: This course is for students who are interested in learning the fundamentals of how generative AI (genAI) works, related tools for business application, and its ethical and responsible use. We will look critically at the ways in which genAI can create and deliver value, its benefits and dangers, and how to critically think about the best uses of the technology.

BUAD 3950.name: Topics in Business - Undergraduate
BUAD 3950.description: Experimental courses offered irregularly at the undergraduate level for the purpose of presenting new subject matter in a particular business field.
BUAD 3950.prereqs: Junior or Senior standing or COB Undergraduate Director permission

BUAD 4000.name: Business, Government, and Society
BUAD 4000.description: An examination of interrelationships between business, society, and government. Explores the legal and ethical significance of transactions in the business decision-making processes. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirements: Sustainability; Navigate.

BUAD 4500.name: Cases and Concepts in Business Policy
BUAD 4500.description: Takes a general manager’s perspective on the administration of the corporation. Topics include the role and responsibility of general management, analysis of threats and opportunities in the competitive environment, strategies for building and sustaining competitive advantage, strategy implementation and management, and strategic management in the international environment. Topics covered through comprehensive case analysis. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirement: Summit.
BUAD 4500.prereqs: INFS 3000, MKTG 3000, FNCE 3050, MGMT 3300, OPTM 3000, ENGL 2080 or ENGL 2090

BUAD 4700.name: Emerging Businesses and Entrepreneurship
BUAD 4700.description: How to plan, organize and operate a new independent business. Case studies of local small businesses.

BUAD 4950.name: Topics in Business - Undergraduate
BUAD 4950.description: Experimental courses offered irregularly at the undergraduate level for the purpose of presenting new subject matter in a particular business field. Second semester junior or senior standing required. Course prerequisites will vary depending upon topics covered.
BUAD 4950.prereqs: Business Students Only and Junior Standing

BUAN 3500.name: Data Visualization and Descriptive Analytics in Business
BUAN 3500.description: This course will provide students with an understanding of how organizations can successfully collect, organize, manipulate, use, prospect and present data. Students will manipulate and interpret actual data using software such as Excel, SPSS, Power BI, Tableau, or Watson. Prereq., INFS 1100, QUAN 2020, Junior Standing, Business Students Only. Course typically offered: Fall, Spring

BUAN 3600.name: Forecasting, Predicting and Planning
BUAN 3600.description: Students will use real world applications to learn how to build forecasting and planning systems. State-of-the-art software will be used to detect interesting patterns and make analytical business decisions.
BUAN 3600.prereqs: INFS 1100, QUAN 2020, Junior Standing, Business Students Only

BUAN 4000.name: Applied Prescriptive Analytics
BUAN 4000.description: This course explores the integration of data within a business context. Students will learn how to move from model parameters to decisions. An emphasis is placed on optimization of business decisions. The course will highlight the application of prescriptive models to decision making in real-world business problems.

BGSO 4000.name: Business, Government and Society
BGSO 4000.description: Examines the interdependence between business, government, and society. Explores the legal and ethical constraints to designing holistic business strategies. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirements: Sustainability; Navigate.

BLAW 2000.name: Business Law
BLAW 2000.description: A study of areas of law of particular importance to business, including contracts, sales, intellectual property, secured transactions, agency, partnerships, limited liability companies, and corporations.  Emphasis is placed on the significance of the law on the decision-making process in business.

CHEM 1001.name: Pre-chemistry
CHEM 1001.description: Preparatory course for the CHEM 1401-1411/1511 General Chemistry sequence. The course emphasizes development of the necessary vocabulary and skill sets for students to transition into a successful General Chemistry experience. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirement: Explore-Physical and Natural World. Course typically offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

CHEM 1002.name: Pre-Chemistry Laboratory
CHEM 1002.description: Optional laboratory course to accompany CHEM 1001. An introduction to chemistry laboratory techniques. Students taking this as an online course will need to purchase a laboratory kit online. See the instructions in the syllabus once the course is made available. International students: Because of potential challenges with shipping lab kits internationally, we do not recommend taking this course while in a foreign country. Approved for the LAS Natural Science requirement and the LAS Natural Science Laboratory requirement.

CHEM 1101.name: Chemistry in the Modern World
CHEM 1101.description: A brief introduction to chemical principles and study of their application to biochemical materials and processes, consumer chemistry, energy problems, air and water pollution and toxic chemicals. This course may be taken with or without the lab course CHEM 1102. Approved for LAS Natural Science area requirement. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirements: Explore-Physical and Natural World; Sustainability. GT-SC2. Course typically offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

CHEM 1102.name: Chemistry in the Modern World Laboratory
CHEM 1102.description: Optional laboratory course designed to complement CHEM 1101. Experiments have been chosen that illustrate the principles discussed in the lecture. Students in this online course will need to purchase a laboratory kit online. See the instructions in the syllabus once the course is made available. International students: Because of potential challenges with shipping lab kits internationally, we do not recommend taking this course while in a foreign country. Approved for LAS Natural Science laboratory requirement. GT-SC1.

CHEM 1111.name: Environmental Science
CHEM 1111.description: Introduction to atomic molecular structure and to biological structure and function. Environmental contaminants in air and their reactions, water quality and its analysis, wastewater treatment, the ecology of natural systems and genetic adaptation. The course deals with worldwide environmental issues in a scientific context. This course may be taken with or without the lab course CHEM 1112. Approved for the LAS Natural Science area and Global Awareness requirements. Approved for Compass Curriculum requirements: Explore: Physical and Natural World; Sustainability. GT-SC2. Course typically offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

CHEM 1112.name: Environmental Science Laboratory
CHEM 1112.description: Optional laboratory course designed to complement CHEM 1111. Students in this online course will need to purchase a laboratory kit online. See the instructions in the syllabus once the course is made available. International students: Because of potential challenges with shipping lab kits internationally, we do not recommend taking this course while in a foreign country. Approved for the LAS Natural Science laboratory requirement. GT-SC1.

CHEM 1121.name: CSI: Forensic Chemistry
